ts-partition-by-type.title: Partition values by runtime type
ts-partition-by-type.description:
A value typed `unknown` must be inspected before it can be used. Practise the basic runtime checks by sorting a mixed
list into buckets.

Write `partitionByType(values)`. `values` is an array of JSON values. Return an object with exactly these keys:

| key | contains |
|---|---|
| `strings` | every string, in original order |
| `numbers` | every number |
| `booleans` | every boolean |
| `arrays` | every array (not searched inside) |
| `objects` | every plain object, that is: not `null` and not an array |
| `nullCount` | how many `null` values were seen (a number) |

Remember the two famous irregularities: `typeof null` is `"object"`, and `typeof []` is `"object"` too.

**Example:** `partitionByType(["a", 1, null, [2], {"k": true}, false])` →
`{"strings":["a"],"numbers":[1],"booleans":[false],"arrays":[[2]],"objects":[{"k":true}],"nullCount":1}`

guide.prereqs: `typeof`, `Array.isArray` and `=== null` from the lesson *Unions, literals and narrowing*.
guide.intuition: Each bucket corresponds to one type guard. The only trick is the order of the checks: `null` and arrays both answer `"object"` to `typeof`, so they must be picked out before the general object check.
hints: Start with an object holding five empty arrays and a counter.
Test `v === null` first, then `Array.isArray(v)`.
Only after those two does `typeof v === "object"` mean a plain object.
guide.brute_force: Filter the list six times, once per bucket. That is correct and O(6n); a single pass with an if/else chain does the same work in one loop.
guide.approach:
Loop once. For each value run the guards from most specific to least: null, array, string, number, boolean, object.

**Dry run** on `["a", null, [2]]`: `"a"` is not null, not an array, `typeof` is string → `strings`. `null` hits the first test → `nullCount` becomes 1. `[2]` is not null, is an array → `arrays`. Result: `strings: ["a"], arrays: [[2]], nullCount: 1`, other buckets empty.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Using truthiness to detect null also catches `0`, `""` and `false`. Checking `typeof v === "object"` first puts null and arrays in the wrong bucket.
guide.follow_up: Add a `Date` bucket using `instanceof`, and think about why its check must also come before the object check.

ts-is-user.title: Type guard: is this a User?
ts-is-user.description:
In TypeScript the function you are about to write would be declared as a **type predicate**:

```typescript
interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string; roles?: string[] }
function isUser(value: unknown): value is User
```

The checker trusts a predicate without verifying its body, so the body has to be right. Write `isUser(value)` returning
`true` only when **all** of these hold:

1. `value` is an object, not `null` and not an array.
2. `value.id` is a number, an integer, and at least 1.
3. `value.name` is a string containing at least one non-space character.
4. If the key `email` is present, it is a string containing the character `@`.
5. If the key `roles` is present, it is an array whose every element is a string (an empty array is fine).

Extra properties are allowed (structural typing). A key that is present with a wrong value (for example `email: null`)
makes the result `false`.

**Examples:** `isUser({"id": 7, "name": "Asha"})` → `true` · `isUser({"id": "7", "name": "Asha"})` → `false` · `isUser(null)` → `false`

guide.prereqs: Type predicates (lesson *Type modifiers*), optional properties (lesson *Objects and structural typing*).
guide.intuition: A guard is a list of ways the data could be wrong, each ruled out in turn. Required fields are checked unconditionally. Optional fields are checked only when the key exists, and existence is asked with `in`, not with truthiness.
hints: Handle `null` and arrays before touching any property.
`Number.isInteger` rejects both non-numbers and fractions.
For an optional field write `if ("email" in value) { ...validate... }`. An empty string is present and invalid.
guide.brute_force: There is no cheaper or dearer algorithm here; the naive version is the one that checks only `id` and `name` with `typeof` and accepts fractional ids, blank names and malformed optional fields.
guide.approach:
Return `false` as soon as any rule fails; return `true` at the end.

**Dry run** on `{id: 1, name: "Tobin", email: ""}`: it is a non-null, non-array object; `id` is the integer 1; `name` trimmed is non-empty; the key `email` is present, it is a string, but it does not contain `@` → `false`. A truthiness test (`if (value.email && ...)`) would have skipped the check because `""` is falsy and wrongly returned `true`.
guide.complexity: Time O(k) where k is the number of roles; space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null === "object"` makes `value.id` throw if null is not excluded. Arrays are objects. `0`, `""` and `null` are falsy, so truthiness cannot tell *absent* from *present but wrong*.
guide.follow_up: Return a list of reasons instead of a boolean, which is the step from a type guard to a schema validator.

ts-narrow-union.title: Narrowing simulator
ts-narrow-union.description:
Simulate what the type checker does when it meets an `if`. You are given a union as a list of **members** and one
**check**; return the members that remain in the true branch and in the false branch.

A member is either a type name, one of `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"bigint"`, `"symbol"`, `"undefined"`, `"null"`,
`"object"`, `"array"`, `"function"`, or a literal written as `{"literal": value}` where value is a string, number or boolean.

Write `narrow(members, check)` returning `{"whenTrue": [...], "whenFalse": [...]}`. Keep members in their original order.

**Checks**

- `{"kind": "typeof", "value": T}` models `typeof x === T`. The runtime `typeof` of a member is its own name, except
  `"null"` → `"object"` and `"array"` → `"object"`; for a literal it is the `typeof` of its value. True branch: members
  whose `typeof` equals `T`. False branch: the others.
- `{"kind": "isArray"}` models `Array.isArray(x)`. True branch: `"array"` only. False branch: the others.
- `{"kind": "truthy"}` models `if (x)`.
  True branch: everything except `"null"`, `"undefined"` and falsy literals (`false`, `0`, `""`).
  False branch: `"null"`, `"undefined"`, the wide primitives that have a falsy value (`"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`,
  `"bigint"`) and falsy literals. (`"object"`, `"array"`, `"function"`, `"symbol"` and truthy literals are never falsy.)
- `{"kind": "equals", "value": V}` models `x === V`, where `V` is a string, number, boolean or `null`.
  If `V` is `null`: true branch is `"null"` only (if present), false branch is everything else.
  Otherwise, true branch: the literal member equal to `V`, and a wide member whose name is `typeof V` is **replaced by**
  `{"literal": V}`; if that produces the same literal twice keep only the first. False branch: every member except the
  literal equal to `V` (wide members stay, since they could hold other values).

**Example:** `narrow(["string", "number", "null"], {"kind": "typeof", "value": "object"})` →
`{"whenTrue": ["null"], "whenFalse": ["string", "number"]}`

guide.prereqs: The narrowing table in *Unions, literals and narrowing*: `typeof`, truthiness, equality, `Array.isArray`.
guide.intuition: Narrowing is filtering. For every member ask two independent questions: *could a value of this member make the check true?* and *could one make it false?* A wide type such as `string` can answer yes to both, so it may appear in both branches.
hints: Write a helper giving the runtime `typeof` of a member, with the two special cases.
For the truthy check, treat literals (decided by their value) separately from names (decided by a fixed list).
For equals, the wide member stays in the false branch and becomes a literal in the true branch; track whether the literal has already been added.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate sample values for each member (for `string`: `""` and `"a"`; for `number`: `0` and `1`, ...) and actually evaluate the check on each sample. It works for a fixed member list but is longer than stating the rules directly.
guide.approach:
Branch on `check.kind`, then loop over members once, pushing each to one or both result lists.

**Dry run**: `narrow(["string", {literal: "a"}, "number"], equals "a")`. `"string"` is the wide type of `"a"`: push `{literal: "a"}` to `whenTrue`, mark added, and keep `"string"` in `whenFalse`. `{literal: "a"}` equals the value but is already added, so it goes nowhere. `"number"` cannot equal `"a"` → `whenFalse`. Result: `whenTrue: [{literal: "a"}]`, `whenFalse: ["string", "number"]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null` and `typeof []` are both `"object"`. The false branch of a truthiness check still contains `string` and `number` because of `""` and `0`. Removing a wide member after `x !== "a"` is wrong: other strings remain.
guide.follow_up: Add an `in` check over object members described by their property lists, or chain several checks.

ts-nullish-defaults.title: Apply defaults with ?? semantics
ts-nullish-defaults.description:
The operator `a ?? b` yields `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. The older idiom `a || b` also replaces `0`, `""`
and `false`, which is a classic source of bugs in configuration code.

Write `withDefaults(config, defaults)` that returns a **new** object:

- For each key in `defaults`: if `config` has no such key, or its value is `null`, use the default value.
- If both the config value and the default value are plain objects (not arrays, not null), apply the same rule
  recursively to them.
- Otherwise keep the config value, even when it is `0`, `""` or `false`.
- Keys that exist only in `config` are copied unchanged.
- If `config` itself is `null`, treat it as `{}`.

**Example:** `withDefaults({"volume": 0, "title": null}, {"volume": 50, "title": "untitled", "loop": true})` →
`{"volume": 0, "title": "untitled", "loop": true}`

guide.prereqs: `??` versus `||` from *Unions, literals and narrowing*; object spread.
guide.intuition: There are exactly two *nullish* values, `null` and `undefined`. A default should replace those and nothing else. Nested objects need the same treatment one level down, which is recursion.
hints: Copy `config` first so keys without defaults survive.
Compare with `=== null || === undefined` (or use `??`), never with `!value`.
Recurse only when both sides are plain objects; arrays are replaced or kept as a whole.
guide.brute_force: `{ ...defaults, ...config }` is the one-liner people reach for. It fails in two ways: an explicit `null` in the config overwrites the default, and nested objects are replaced wholesale instead of merged.
guide.approach:
Start from a shallow copy of the config; walk the keys of `defaults` and decide per key.

**Dry run** with config `{theme: {size: 0}}` and defaults `{theme: {size: 14, colour: "navy"}, wrap: true}`. Key `theme`: both plain objects → recurse; inside, `size` is `0` (not nullish) → keep `0`; `colour` missing → `"navy"`. Key `wrap`: missing → `true`. Result `{theme: {size: 0, colour: "navy"}, wrap: true}`.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(total number of keys in both objects).
guide.pitfalls: `||` discards `0`, `""` and `false`. `typeof [] === "object"`, so exclude arrays from the recursive case. Mutating `config` instead of copying surprises callers.
guide.follow_up: In TypeScript the return type could be written `T & Required<Pick<D, keyof D>>`; try expressing it.

ts-is-assignable.title: Structural assignability checker
ts-is-assignable.description:
Implement the heart of a type checker: *is a value of type `source` allowed where type `target` is expected?*
Types are given as plain **descriptors**:

| descriptor | meaning |
|---|---|
| `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"null"`, `"undefined"` | primitives |
| `"any"`, `"unknown"`, `"never"` | the special types |
| `{"kind": "literal", "value": v}` | literal type; `v` is a string, number or boolean |
| `{"kind": "array", "element": T}` | `T[]` |
| `{"kind": "object", "props": {name: {"type": T, "optional": bool}}}` | object type (`optional` may be omitted, meaning required) |
| `{"kind": "union", "members": [T, ...]}` | `A | B | ...` |

Write `isAssignable(source, target)` returning a boolean. Apply these rules **in this order**; the first that matches decides:

1. `source` is `"never"` → `true`.
2. `source` is `"any"` → `true` unless `target` is `"never"`.
3. `target` is `"any"` or `"unknown"` → `true`.
4. `source` is a union → `true` only if **every** member is assignable to `target`.
5. `target` is a union → `true` if `source` is assignable to **some** member.
6. `source` is `"unknown"` → `false`. `target` is `"never"` → `false`.
7. Both are primitive names → `true` only if they are the same name.
8. `source` is a literal → assignable to an equal literal (same value, compared with `===`) and to the primitive name that
   equals `typeof value`; otherwise `false`.
9. Both are arrays → compare the element types (arrays are treated covariantly, as TypeScript does).
10. Both are objects → for every property of `target`: if `source` has it, the source property type must be assignable
    to the target property type, **and** an optional source property is not assignable to a required target property;
    if `source` lacks it, the target property must be optional. Extra source properties are fine.
11. Anything else → `false`.

**Examples:** `isAssignable({"kind":"literal","value":"north"}, "string")` → `true` ·
`isAssignable("string", {"kind":"literal","value":"north"})` → `false`

guide.prereqs: The set model of types (*The type system*), structural typing and optional properties (*Objects and structural typing*), `any`/`unknown`/`never` (*Type modifiers*).
guide.intuition: Assignability asks whether every value of the source is also a value of the target. Each rule is that one question specialised: a union source needs *all* of its members to fit; a union target needs *one* member to accept; an object source needs to supply everything the target requires.
hints: Deal with the special names first; they short-circuit everything else.
Handle a union on the source side before a union on the target side.
For objects, loop over the *target's* properties, never the source's: extra source properties do not matter.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate sample values of the source type and test each against the target. That works for literals and tiny unions but cannot enumerate `string`, so a rule-based recursive comparison is the practical solution.
guide.approach:
A recursive function with the eleven rules as a chain of early returns.

**Dry run**: source `{name?: string}`, target `{name: string}`. Neither is special, neither is a union, both are objects. Target property `name`: the source has it; the source's is optional while the target's is required → `false`. (A value `{}` is a valid source but lacks the required `name`.)

**Second dry run**: source `"a" | "b"`, target `string`. Source is a union: is `"a"` assignable to `string`? Literal, `typeof "a"` is `"string"` → yes. Same for `"b"` → `true`.
guide.complexity: Time O(size of source × size of target) in the worst case because of unions; space O(depth) for recursion.
guide.pitfalls: Checking the target union before the source union gives wrong answers for union-to-union. `any` is assignable to everything except `never`. An empty union behaves like `never` as a source and accepts nothing as a target. Using `==` for literals makes `1` equal `"1"`.
guide.follow_up: Add function types with contravariant parameters (see the problem *Function assignability and variance*) and excess property checking for a `fresh` flag on object descriptors.

ts-cart-reducer.title: Discriminated-union reducer
ts-cart-reducer.description:
A shopping cart is driven by **actions**, objects tagged with a `type` property. In TypeScript:

```typescript
type Action =
  | { type: "add"; sku: string; qty?: number }
  | { type: "remove"; sku: string }
  | { type: "setQty"; sku: string; qty: number }
  | { type: "applyCoupon"; code: string }
  | { type: "clear" };
```

Write `runCart(actions)`. Start from the state `{ items: {}, coupon: null }` and apply the actions in order:

- `add`: increase `items[sku]` by `qty` (default `1` when `qty` is missing), creating the entry at that quantity if needed.
- `remove`: delete `items[sku]`; do nothing if it is not there.
- `setQty`: set `items[sku]` to `qty`; if `qty` is `0` or negative, delete the entry instead.
- `applyCoupon`: set `coupon` to `code` (a later coupon replaces an earlier one).
- `clear`: empty `items` and reset `coupon` to `null`.

Return `{ "items": ..., "coupon": ..., "totalQty": sum of all quantities }`.

If an action has any other `type`, stop immediately and return `{ "error": "Unhandled action: <type>" }`. This is the
runtime half of an exhaustiveness check.

**Example:** `runCart([{"type":"add","sku":"tea"},{"type":"add","sku":"tea","qty":2}])` →
`{"items":{"tea":3},"coupon":null,"totalQty":3}`

guide.prereqs: Discriminated unions and `assertNever` (*Objects and structural typing*); reducers (*Typing React and Express*).
guide.intuition: A reducer is a function `(state, action) => newState`. The `type` tag tells you which variant you hold, and a `switch` gives each variant its own branch. The `default` branch is where anything unexpected lands.
hints: Write the inner `reduce(state, action)` first; `runCart` is then a loop around it.
Use `action.qty ?? 1` for the default quantity.
Throw in `default` and catch in `runCart` to produce the error object.
guide.brute_force: A chain of `if`/`else if` that mutates one state object works too. It is the same complexity; the `switch` over the tag is clearer and maps directly onto TypeScript's narrowing.
guide.approach:
Fold the action list with the reducer, then compute `totalQty` from the final items.

**Dry run** on `[add a ×2, add b ×3, remove a, add c]`: after 1 → `{a: 2}`; after 2 → `{a: 2, b: 3}`; after 3 → `{b: 3}`; after 4 → `{b: 3, c: 1}` (default quantity). `totalQty` = 4, coupon stays `null`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n × k) with copying (k = distinct items), or O(n) if you mutate a private state; space O(k).
guide.pitfalls: `setQty` with 0 must delete the key, not store 0. `clear` resets the coupon too. Silently ignoring an unknown action hides bugs: the tests expect an error.
guide.follow_up: Add an `undo` action by keeping a history stack of previous states, which is easy precisely because the reducer returns new objects instead of mutating.

ts-exhaustive-check.title: Exhaustive switch checker
ts-exhaustive-check.description:
The compiler's exhaustiveness check answers: *does this `switch` handle every member of the union?* Reproduce it over
plain data.

Write `checkExhaustive(variants, cases, hasDefault)`:

- `variants`: the tags of the union, for example `["circle", "rect", "triangle"]` (no duplicates).
- `cases`: the labels written in the `switch`, in source order (may contain duplicates or labels that are not variants).
- `hasDefault`: whether the `switch` has a `default:` branch.

Return an object:

- `missing`: variants with no `case`, in the order of `variants`;
- `unknown`: case labels that are not variants, each once, in order of first appearance;
- `duplicates`: case labels that appear more than once, each once, in order of first appearance;
- `exhaustive`: `true` if `hasDefault` is true or `missing` is empty.

**Example:** `checkExhaustive(["circle","rect","triangle"], ["rect","circle"], false)` →
`{"missing":["triangle"],"unknown":[],"duplicates":[],"exhaustive":false}`

guide.prereqs: Exhaustiveness checking with `never` (*Objects and structural typing*); `Set`.
guide.intuition: Exhaustiveness is set difference: the variants minus the handled labels must be empty. The two other lists are the reverse difference (labels that are not variants) and a duplicate count.
hints: `missing` is a filter over `variants`.
Walk `cases` once with a `seen` set to find duplicates.
A `default` branch makes the switch exhaustive no matter what is missing.
guide.brute_force: Nested loops comparing every variant with every case: O(v × c). Fine for a handful of tags, and sets bring it down to O(v + c).
guide.approach:
Build a set of case labels and a set of variants; filter and scan.

**Dry run**: variants `[a, b]`, cases `[a, c, b, c, d]`, no default. `missing`: both `a` and `b` are handled → `[]`. Scan: `a` known; `c` unknown → `[c]`; `b` known; `c` seen before → duplicates `[c]`; `d` unknown → `[c, d]`. `exhaustive` is `true` because nothing is missing.
guide.complexity: Time O(v + c) with sets (the small `includes` calls are on the output lists), space O(v + c).
guide.pitfalls: Reporting a label three times when it appears three times. Forgetting the `default` rule. Deciding exhaustiveness by comparing lengths, which duplicates and unknown labels defeat.
guide.follow_up: In real TypeScript an unknown label is itself a compile error (`Type '"x"' is not comparable to type ...`). The typed lint rule `switch-exhaustiveness-check` reports the `missing` list.

ts-overload-dispatch.title: Overload-style dispatch
ts-overload-dispatch.description:
TypeScript overloads list several call signatures, but after compilation only **one** implementation exists, and it has
to work out at runtime which signature was used. Write that implementation.

`describeArgs(args)` receives the argument list as an array and must behave like a function with these overloads,
tried from top to bottom:

| # | arguments | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `(n: number)` | `"num:"` + `n.toFixed(2)` |
| 2 | `(s: string)` | `"str:"` + `s` trimmed and upper-cased |
| 3 | `(a: number, b: number)` | `"range:"` + smaller + `".."` + larger |
| 4 | `(s: string, times: number)` where `times` is an integer ≥ 0 | `"repeat:"` + `s` repeated `times` times joined with `"-"` |
| 5 | `(list: unknown[])` (exactly one argument, an array) | `"list:"` + its length |

If no overload matches, return `"TypeError: no overload matches (" + tags + ")"` where `tags` is the comma-and-space
separated list of each argument's tag: `"null"`, `"array"`, or its `typeof` (`"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"object"`).
With zero arguments the tag list is empty: `"TypeError: no overload matches ()"`.

**Examples:** `describeArgs([3.14159])` → `"num:3.14"` · `describeArgs(["ab", 3])` → `"repeat:ab-ab-ab"` ·
`describeArgs([true, 1])` → `"TypeError: no overload matches (boolean, number)"`

guide.prereqs: Overload signatures and why only the implementation survives compilation (*Functions, arrays and tuples*).
guide.intuition: Each overload is a pattern over the *count* and *runtime types* of the arguments. Compute a tag for every argument once, then compare the tag list against each pattern in order.
hints: Write `tag(v)` returning `null`, `array` or `typeof v`.
Branch on `args.length` first; it halves the cases.
Overload 4 has a value condition as well as a type condition: `Number.isInteger(times) && times >= 0`.
guide.brute_force: A long chain of `typeof` tests on `args[0]` and `args[1]` without checking the length. It mis-handles extra arguments and treats `null` and plain objects as arrays.
guide.approach:
Tags, then a decision table.

**Dry run** on `["x", 2.5]`: tags `[string, number]`, length 2. Overload 3 needs two numbers: no. Overload 4 needs string + non-negative integer: `2.5` is not an integer: no. Nothing else has two parameters → `"TypeError: no overload matches (string, number)"`.
guide.complexity: Time O(k) for k arguments (plus the length of the repeated string), space O(k).
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null` and `typeof []` are `"object"`. `Array(2.5)` throws a RangeError, so validate before building. Ignoring the argument count lets `(1, 2, 3)` match the range overload.
guide.follow_up: Write the five overload signatures in TypeScript and check that the two-argument call `("x", 2.5)` compiles even though it fails at runtime: types cannot express "integer".

tests.expected: TypeError: no overload matches (number, number, number)

ts-tuple-zip.title: Zip lists into tuples
ts-tuple-zip.description:
`zip` pairs up the elements of several lists by position. In TypeScript its result is an array of **tuples**:
`zip([1, 2], ["a", "b"])` has type `[number, string][]`.

Write `zip(lists)` where `lists` is an array of arrays. Return an array whose `i`-th entry is the tuple
`[lists[0][i], lists[1][i], ...]`. Stop at the length of the **shortest** list. With no lists at all, return `[]`.

**Examples:** `zip([[1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]])` → `[[1, "a"], [2, "b"], [3, "c"]]` ·
`zip([[1, 2, 3], ["a"]])` → `[[1, "a"]]`

guide.prereqs: Tuples versus arrays (*Functions, arrays and tuples*).
guide.intuition: The result has one row per position, and a position only exists if every list has it, hence the shortest length. Each row collects the element at that position from every list.
hints: Find the minimum length first.
Row `i` is `lists.map((list) => list[i])`.
`Math.min()` with no arguments is `Infinity`, so handle the empty input separately.
guide.brute_force: Loop while every list still has an element at index `i`, checking all lists on every step: the same O(n × k) work, with the stopping test repeated.
guide.approach:
Compute `length`, loop `i` from 0 to `length - 1`, push a row.

**Dry run** on `[[1, 2, 3], ["a"]]`: lengths 3 and 1 → `length` 1. `i = 0`: row `[1, "a"]`. Done: `[[1, "a"]]`.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n × k) for k lists of shortest length n.
guide.pitfalls: Mapping over the first list instead of the shortest pads rows with `undefined`. An empty outer list makes `Math.min(...[])` return `Infinity` and the loop never ends.
guide.follow_up: Type it in TypeScript for two lists: `function zip<A, B>(a: A[], b: B[]): [A, B][]`. The variadic version uses a mapped tuple type: `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K][] }`.

ts-head-tail.title: Head, tail, init and last

guide.prereqs: Array indexing and `slice`; `T | undefined` for possibly missing elements (*Functions, arrays and tuples*).
guide.intuition: Four views of the same list. The only decision is what to do when there is nothing to view.
hints: Handle the empty list first.
`slice(1)` drops the first element; `slice(0, n - 1)` drops the last.
Do not use `||` to supply `null`: the first element may legitimately be `0` or `false`.
guide.brute_force: Build `tail` and `init` with loops that push elements one at a time. Same complexity, more code.
guide.approach:
One early return, then four expressions.

**Dry run** on `[0, false]`: not empty. `head` = `0`, `tail` = `[false]`, `init` = `[0]`, `last` = `false`. A version using `list[0] || null` would report `head: null`, which is wrong.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n) for the two copies.
guide.pitfalls: Falsy elements and `||`. Off-by-one in the `init` slice. Returning the same array object for `tail` when the caller expects a copy.
guide.follow_up: Write the type-level `Head<T>` and `Tail<T>` from the lesson *Interview essentials II* and compare.

ts-get-path.title: Get by key path with a default
ts-get-path.description:
`obj?.a?.b?.[0] ?? fallback` reads a nested value safely when the path is known while writing the code. Write the
version for a path that arrives as a string.

`getPath(source, path, fallback)`:

- `path` uses dots and brackets: `"crew[0].name"`, `"a.b.c"`, `"[1][0]"`, `"grid[2][3]"`. Split it into keys; a key is
  any run of characters other than `.`, `[` and `]`. The empty path `""` has no keys.
- Start at `source` and follow the keys one at a time. A step is only possible when the current value is an object or
  an array **and** has the key as its **own** property (so `"toString"` or `"constructor"` is never found).
- If any step is impossible, return `fallback`.
- If every step succeeds, return the value found. A found `null` is returned as `null` (it exists); only "not found"
  produces the fallback.
- With the empty path, return `source` itself.

**Examples:** `getPath({"crew": [{"name": "Asha"}]}, "crew[0].name", "?")` → `"Asha"` ·
`getPath({"a": {"b": null}}, "a.b", "?")` → `null` · `getPath({"a": 1}, "a.b.c", "?")` → `"?"`

guide.prereqs: Optional chaining and `??` (*Unions, literals and narrowing*); `keyof` and indexed access (*Type modifiers*).
guide.intuition: Turn the path into a list of keys, then walk. At each step there are two questions: *can I look inside the current value at all?* and *does it really have this key?* A "no" to either ends the walk with the fallback.
hints: A regular expression matching runs of characters that are not `.`, `[` or `]` extracts the keys.
Use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, key)` (or `Object.hasOwn`) so inherited members are not found.
Return `current` as is at the end: do not apply `||` or `??`, because a found `0`, `false`, `""` or `null` is a real answer.
guide.brute_force: `path.split(".")` handles dotted paths only, and `current?.[key]` with a final `|| fallback` loses falsy values and finds inherited members. Each shortcut fails some of the tests.
guide.approach:
Parse, loop, check, step.

**Dry run**: `getPath({crew: [{name: "Asha"}]}, "crew[0].name", "?")`. Keys: `crew`, `0`, `name`. `crew` is an own key of the object → the array. `0` is an own key of the array → `{name: "Asha"}`. `name` is an own key → `"Asha"`. Returned.

**Second**: `getPath({a: {b: null}}, "a.b.c", "?")`: after `a`, `b` the current value is `null`; the next step cannot look inside `null` → `"?"`.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of path), space O(number of keys).
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null === "object"`. Strings have a `length` but are primitives, so the rule here says no step into them. Arrays do own `length`. Applying the fallback to found falsy values.
guide.follow_up: In TypeScript the path can be typed with template literal types so that only valid paths compile; libraries such as react-hook-form do this.

ts-result-chain.title: Result container with map and flatMap
ts-result-chain.description:
A `Result<T, E>` is the generic discriminated union `{ ok: true, value: T } | { ok: false, error: E }`. Implement its
core operations and run a pipeline through them.

Write `runResult(start, ops)`. Begin with `{ ok: true, value: start }` (`start` is a number) and apply each operation
in order. An operation is an array `[name, argument]`:

| operation | effect |
|---|---|
| `["map", fn]` | on success, replace the value with `fn(value)`; on failure, do nothing |
| `["flatMap", fn]` | on success, replace the whole result with `fn(value)`, which is itself a Result; on failure, do nothing |
| `["mapErr", fn]` | on failure, replace the error with `fn(error)`; on success, do nothing |
| `["orElse", n]` | on failure, become `{ ok: true, value: n }`; on success, do nothing |

`fn` is the **name** of a function from these tables.

`map` functions: `"inc"` (x + 1), `"double"` (x × 2), `"square"` (x × x), `"negate"` (−x), `"half"` (x ÷ 2).

`flatMap` functions (each returns a Result):
`"sqrt"`: error `"negative input"` when x < 0, otherwise success with `Math.sqrt(x)`;
`"reciprocal"`: error `"division by zero"` when x is 0, otherwise success with `1 / x`;
`"even"`: error `"not even"` unless x is an even integer, otherwise success with x unchanged.

`mapErr` functions: `"upper"` (the message in upper case), `"tag"` (`"E:"` + message).

Return the final Result object.

**Examples:** `runResult(3, [["map", "inc"], ["flatMap", "sqrt"]])` → `{"ok": true, "value": 2}` ·
`runResult(0, [["flatMap", "reciprocal"], ["map", "double"]])` → `{"ok": false, "error": "division by zero"}`

guide.prereqs: Generic discriminated unions and the `Result` type (*Generics*, *Interview essentials II*).
guide.intuition: A Result travels along one of two tracks, success or failure. `map` and `flatMap` act only on the success track; `mapErr` and `orElse` act only on the failure track. Once on the failure track, success operations are skipped, so the first error is carried to the end unless `orElse` switches tracks.
hints: Keep three lookup tables from name to function.
`map` wraps the function's answer in a new success; `flatMap` uses the function's answer as the new result.
Every operation starts with a test of `result.ok`.
guide.brute_force: Use exceptions: compute with plain numbers and `throw` on errors, catching at `orElse`. It works, but it is exactly the style the Result type replaces, and it makes `mapErr` awkward.
guide.approach:
Loop over the operations, updating one `result` variable.

**Dry run**: `runResult(7, [flatMap even, orElse 0, map inc])`. Start `ok(7)`. `even`: 7 is odd → `err("not even")`. `orElse 0`: on the failure track → `ok(0)`. `map inc` → `ok(1)`. With start 8 the first step stays `ok(8)`, `orElse` is skipped, and the answer is `ok(9)`.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of operations), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Wrapping the output of a `flatMap` function in another success gives a Result inside a Result. Calling a `map` function on a failure reads `result.value`, which is `undefined`, and produces `NaN`.
guide.follow_up: Give it TypeScript signatures: `map<T, U, E>(r: Result<T, E>, f: (t: T) => U): Result<U, E>`. Then write `Option<T>` (some or none) the same way.

ts-event-bus.title: Event bus with typed channels
ts-event-bus.description:
In TypeScript an event bus is typed by a map from channel name to payload type:

```typescript
interface Bus<Events> {
  on<K extends keyof Events>(channel: K, listener: (payload: Events[K]) => void): void;
  emit<K extends keyof Events>(channel: K, payload: Events[K]): void;
}
```

The compiler then rejects unknown channels and wrong payloads. Build the runtime equivalent, which checks the same
two things while running.

Write `runBus(channels, ops)`. `channels` maps each channel name to its payload type, one of `"string"`, `"number"`,
`"boolean"`, `"object"` (a non-null, non-array object). `ops` is a list of operations; return the list of their results.

| operation | result |
|---|---|
| `["on", channel, id]` | subscribe listener `id`; result `"ok"`. Subscribing an id already on that channel changes nothing (still `"ok"`). |
| `["once", channel, id]` | like `on`, but the listener is removed after its first delivery |
| `["off", channel, id]` | unsubscribe; result `true` if it was subscribed, otherwise `false` |
| `["emit", channel, payload]` | deliver to every listener of the channel in subscription order; result is the list of strings `id + ":" + JSON.stringify(payload)` (an empty list if nobody listens) |

Errors: `on`, `once` and `emit` on a channel that is not in `channels` give `"error: unknown channel"`; `off` on an
unknown channel gives `false`. `emit` with a payload of the wrong type gives `"error: expected <type>"` and delivers
nothing (so `once` listeners stay subscribed).

**Example:** `runBus({"tick": "number"}, [["on","tick","a"], ["emit","tick",1], ["emit","tick","x"]])` →
`["ok", ["a:1"], "error: expected number"]`

guide.prereqs: `keyof` constraints and indexed access types (*Generics*); runtime type checks (*Unions, literals and narrowing*).
guide.intuition: The channel map plays the role of the `Events` type. Each operation first asks the two questions the compiler would ask (does the channel exist? does the payload fit?), then does the bookkeeping on a list of listeners per channel.
hints: Store, per channel, an ordered array of `{ id, once }`.
Check the channel with an own-property test so that names like `constructor` are not treated as known.
On a successful emit, build the result from the current listeners and then drop the `once` ones.
guide.brute_force: One flat array of `{ channel, id, once }` records filtered on every operation. It is O(total listeners) per operation and still passes; a map from channel to list avoids scanning unrelated channels.
guide.approach:
Initialise an empty list per channel, then process the operations in order.

**Dry run**: channels `{msg: string}`, ops `once msg a`, `emit msg 7`, `emit msg "ok"`, `emit msg "again"`. `once` → `"ok"`, listeners `[a(once)]`. `emit 7`: wrong type → `"error: expected string"`, nothing delivered, `a` stays. `emit "ok"` → `["a:\"ok\""]`, then `a` is removed. `emit "again"` → `[]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(listeners on the channel) per operation, space O(total listeners).
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null` and `typeof []` are `"object"`. A failed emit must not consume `once` listeners. `channels[name]` is truthy for inherited names such as `toString` on a plain object.
guide.follow_up: Write the TypeScript class `Bus<Events extends Record<string, unknown>>` whose `emit` only compiles for a valid channel and payload pair.

ts-strict-flags.title: Expand the strict flag
ts-strict-flags.description:
In `tsconfig.json`, `"strict": true` switches on a family of eight checks, and each member can still be set
individually. An individual setting always wins over `strict`.

The family: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`,
`strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitThis`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `alwaysStrict`.

Write `effectiveFlags(compilerOptions)` returning an object with exactly those eight keys, each `true` or `false`:

- if the flag is set in `compilerOptions` (to `true` or `false`), use that value;
- otherwise use the value of `compilerOptions.strict`, or `false` when `strict` is not set.

Ignore every other option.

**Example:** `effectiveFlags({"strict": true, "strictPropertyInitialization": false})` → all eight `true` except
`strictPropertyInitialization: false`.

guide.prereqs: The strict family (*Configuration: tsconfig.json and the strictness flags*).
guide.intuition: `strict` is a default for eight switches. A switch that was set by hand keeps its own value; a switch that was not set takes the default. The subtle case is a switch set by hand to `false`.
hints: Keep the family in an array and loop over it.
Decide "was it set?" with `typeof value === "boolean"`, not with truthiness.
`strict` missing means the default is `false`.
guide.brute_force: Write eight separate lines such as `noImplicitAny: o.noImplicitAny ?? o.strict ?? false`. It works and is repetitive; a loop over the list of names says the same thing once.
guide.approach:
Compute the default, then fill in each flag.

**Dry run** on `{strict: true, strictPropertyInitialization: false}`: default is `true`. Seven flags are not set → `true`. `strictPropertyInitialization` is a boolean (`false`) → keep `false`. Using `o[f] || o.strict` here would turn that `false` back into `true`, which is the bug to avoid.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(1): always eight flags.
guide.pitfalls: `||` cannot distinguish "explicitly false" from "not set". Returning unrelated options such as `target`.
guide.follow_up: `tsc --showConfig` prints the real effective configuration; compare its output with yours for a project.

ts-tsconfig-extends.title: Resolve a tsconfig extends chain
ts-tsconfig-extends.description:
A `tsconfig.json` can inherit from another with `"extends"`. Implement the inheritance rules.

`resolveConfig(configs, name)`: `configs` maps a file name to its configuration object; `name` is the one to resolve.
A configuration may contain `extends` (the name of its parent), `compilerOptions` (an object), `include`, `exclude`,
`files` and `references` (arrays).

Rules:

1. If the configuration has `extends`, first resolve the parent (which may itself extend another).
2. `compilerOptions`: merged **key by key**; the child's value wins. The result always has a `compilerOptions`
   object, possibly empty.
3. `include`, `exclude`, `files`: if the child defines the key, it **replaces** the parent's list entirely (even with an
   empty list); otherwise the parent's list is inherited. A key nobody defines is absent from the result.
4. `references` is **not inherited**: the result has `references` only if the configuration named `name` defines it.
5. The result never contains `extends`.

Errors, returned as `{"error": message}`:

- a name (the starting one or any parent) that is not in `configs`: `"cannot find <name>"`;
- a cycle: `"circular extends: "` followed by the chain of names from the start, joined with `" -> "` and ending with
  the repeated name, for example `"circular extends: a -> b -> a"`.

**Example:** with `base = {compilerOptions: {strict: true, target: "ES2022"}, include: ["src", "types"]}` and
`api = {extends: "base", compilerOptions: {strict: false, outDir: "dist"}, include: ["src"]}`,
`resolveConfig(configs, "api")` → `{"compilerOptions": {"strict": false, "target": "ES2022", "outDir": "dist"}, "include": ["src"]}`

guide.prereqs: The `extends` rules in *Configuration: tsconfig.json and the strictness flags*.
guide.intuition: Inheritance is a chain: grandparent, parent, child. Lay the chain out from the most distant ancestor to the requested file and apply each layer on top of the previous one. Different keys have different stacking rules: options blend, file lists replace, references do not travel.
hints: First walk upward collecting the names; that walk is also where missing files and cycles are detected.
Reverse the chain, then fold: `Object.assign` for `compilerOptions`, plain assignment for the three lists.
Add `references` at the end from the requested configuration only.
guide.brute_force: Recursion: resolve the parent, then merge the child onto it. Equivalent in cost; it needs a `seen` list passed down to detect cycles and to build the error message.
guide.approach:
Two phases: collect the chain, then apply it root first.

**Dry run** for `api-test` (extends `api`, which extends `base`). Chain collected: `api-test`, `api`, `base`; reversed: `base`, `api`, `api-test`. After `base`: options `{target, strict: true, skipLibCheck}`, include `[src, types]`. After `api`: `strict` becomes `false`, `outDir` added, include replaced by `[src]`. After `api-test`: `noEmit` added, `exclude: [dist]` set, include still `[src]`. References: only `api-test`'s own; `base`'s reference to `../shared` is not inherited.
guide.complexity: Time O(chain length × options), space O(chain length + options).
guide.pitfalls: `{...parent, ...child}` replaces the whole `compilerOptions` object. Concatenating `include` lists. Inheriting `references`. An empty `include: []` in the child still replaces the parent's list. A config that extends itself.
guide.follow_up: Real `extends` also accepts an array of parents (TypeScript 5.0 and later), applied left to right. Extend your solution to support it.

expected.error: circular extends: loop-a -> loop-b -> loop-c -> loop-a
circular extends: loop-b -> loop-c -> loop-a -> loop-b

ts-enum-reverse.title: Compile an enum with reverse mapping
ts-enum-reverse.description:
A TypeScript `enum` compiles to a real object. Numeric members get entries in **both** directions (name → number and
number → name, the *reverse mapping*); string members get only name → value.

Write `buildEnum(members)` that produces that object. Each member is either

- a string `"Name"`: a member without an initialiser, or
- a pair `["Name", value]` where `value` is a number or a string.

Rules:

1. A member without an initialiser gets `0` if it is the first member, otherwise the previous member's numeric value
   plus one.
2. If the previous member has a **string** value, a member without an initialiser is an error: return
   `{"error": "Enum member must have initializer: <Name>"}` (for the first such member).
3. For a numeric member store `result[name] = number` and `result[String(number)] = name`. If two members share a
   number, the later one wins the reverse entry.
4. For a string member store only `result[name] = value`.

**Examples:** `buildEnum(["Low", "High"])` → `{"Low": 0, "High": 1, "0": "Low", "1": "High"}` ·
`buildEnum([["Port", "red"]])` → `{"Port": "red"}`

guide.prereqs: What an enum compiles to (*Syntax extensions*).
guide.intuition: Walk the members while remembering one thing: the last numeric value. It supplies the next automatic value, and its absence (after a string member) is what makes a bare member illegal.
hints: Use a variable `previous` that starts at −1, so the first automatic value is 0.
After a string member set `previous` to `null`.
Only numeric members get the second, reverse entry.
guide.brute_force: Number the members by their index. It gives the right answer only when no member has an initialiser; the moment one says `= 200`, the following members must continue from 201.
guide.approach:
One pass.

**Dry run** on `[["Ok", 200], "Created", ["NotFound", 404], "Gone"]`: `Ok` = 200, reverse `"200"` → `Ok`, previous 200. `Created` has no initialiser → 201. `NotFound` = 404. `Gone` → 405. Eight entries in total.

For `[["Port", "red"], "Starboard"]`: `Port` is a string member, previous becomes `null`; `Starboard` has no initialiser → error.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Adding reverse entries for string members (TypeScript does not, and they could collide with member names). Using the index as the value. Forgetting that a numeric member after a string member re-enables automatic values.
guide.follow_up: `Object.keys` of a numeric enum returns names and numbers mixed. Write `enumNames(e)` that returns only the member names.

expected.error: Enum member must have initializer: Starboard
Enum member must have initializer: C

ts-pick-omit.title: Runtime Pick and Omit
ts-pick-omit.description:
`Pick<T, K>` and `Omit<T, K>` change a **type**; nothing happens to the object at runtime. When you really need a
smaller object (to strip a password before sending a response, say) you need the value-level versions.

Write `pickOmit(mode, source, keys)`:

- `mode` is `"pick"` or `"omit"`.
- `"pick"`: return a new object with only the listed keys that `source` actually has as own properties. Listed keys
  that `source` lacks are skipped (they do **not** appear with `undefined`).
- `"omit"`: return a new object with every own key of `source` except the listed ones.
- Values are copied as they are (a shallow copy). Duplicate keys in `keys` have no extra effect.

**Examples:** `pickOmit("pick", {"id": 1, "name": "Asha", "hash": "x"}, ["id", "name"])` → `{"id": 1, "name": "Asha"}` ·
`pickOmit("omit", {"id": 1, "name": "Asha", "hash": "x"}, ["hash"])` → `{"id": 1, "name": "Asha"}`

guide.prereqs: `Pick` and `Omit` as mapped types (*Type operations*).
guide.intuition: Both operations are a filter over the object's own keys. The only difference is whether "listed" means keep or drop.
hints: Iterate over `Object.keys(source)`, not over `keys`: that automatically skips keys the object lacks.
A `Set` makes the membership test O(1).
Never test the *value* to decide whether to keep a key: `null`, `0` and `false` are legitimate values.
guide.brute_force: For `pick`, loop over `keys` and copy `source[key]`. It creates entries for keys the object does not have, and reads inherited members such as `constructor`.
guide.approach:
Build a set of listed keys and filter.

**Dry run**: `pickOmit("pick", {id: 1}, ["id", "missing"])`. Own keys: `id`. Listed? yes, and mode is pick → keep. `missing` is never visited because the object does not own it. Result `{id: 1}`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n + k) for n own keys and k listed keys; space O(n + k).
guide.pitfalls: Emitting `undefined`/`null` for missing keys. Dropping falsy values. Mutating `source` with `delete`.
guide.follow_up: Type it: `function pick<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(source: T, keys: K[]): Pick<T, K>`.

ts-required-keys.title: Runtime Required and Partial check
ts-required-keys.description:
`Required<T>` says every key must be present; `Partial<T>` says every key may be absent. A real type mixes both.
Check an object against such a description at runtime.

Write `checkRequired(value, spec)`. `spec` maps each known key to `"required"` or `"optional"`. Return:

- `missing`: required keys that `value` does not have as own properties, sorted alphabetically;
- `extra`: own keys of `value` that are not in `spec`, sorted alphabetically (this mirrors excess property checking);
- `ok`: `true` when both lists are empty.

A key whose value is `null`, `0`, `""` or `false` **is present**.

**Example:** `checkRequired({"id": 1, "nick": null, "age": 3}, {"id": "required", "name": "required", "nick": "optional"})` →
`{"missing": ["name"], "extra": ["age"], "ok": false}`

guide.prereqs: Optional properties and excess property checking (*Objects and structural typing*); `Required`/`Partial` (*Type operations*).
guide.intuition: Two set differences. Required keys minus the keys the object has gives `missing`; the object's keys minus the known keys gives `extra`.
hints: Presence is about the key, so use an own-property test.
Sort both lists before returning.
Optional keys never appear in `missing`.
guide.brute_force: Nested loops comparing every spec key with every object key: O(n × m). Own-property lookups make each test O(1).
guide.approach:
Filter the spec's keys, filter the value's keys, sort.

**Dry run** on value `{id: 1, nick: null, age: 3}` and spec `{id: required, name: required, nick: optional}`: `id` present; `name` required and absent → missing; `nick` optional, skip. Value keys: `id` known, `nick` known (present even though `null`), `age` unknown → extra. `ok` is `false`.
guide.complexity: Time O((n + m) log(n + m)) because of sorting; space O(n + m).
guide.pitfalls: Truthiness reports `0`, `""`, `false` and `null` as missing. `spec[k]` is truthy for inherited names like `toString`.
guide.follow_up: Add a third status `"forbidden"`, or nest specs to check sub-objects.

ts-deep-freeze.title: Deep freeze: a runtime DeepReadonly
ts-deep-freeze.description:
`Readonly<T>` and `as const` protect data only while compiling. `Object.freeze` protects at runtime, but only one level
deep. Combine the two ideas.

Write `deepFreeze(value)`:

- If `value` is an object or an array, freeze it **and everything reachable inside it** (nested objects and arrays at
  any depth), then return the **same** reference (do not copy).
- Any other value (number, string, boolean, `null`) is returned unchanged.

The provided driver `freezeReport(value, mutations)` calls your `deepFreeze`, then attempts each mutation in strict
mode, where writing to a frozen object throws. A mutation is `[path, replacement]`: follow `path` (a list of keys) and
assign `replacement` to the last key. The driver returns

`{ "sameReference": ..., "blocked": number of mutations that threw, "value": the object afterwards }`.

If your freeze is complete, every mutation is blocked and `value` is unchanged.

**Example:** `freezeReport({"a": {"b": 1}}, [[["a", "b"], 2], [["c"], 3]])` →
`{"sameReference": true, "blocked": 2, "value": {"a": {"b": 1}}}`

guide.prereqs: `readonly`, `as const` and why they are compile-time only (*Interfaces and classes*, *Type modifiers*); shallow versus deep utility types (*Type operations*).
guide.intuition: Freezing is like `Readonly<T>`: one level. To get `DeepReadonly<T>` you repeat the operation on every value inside, which is recursion over the object tree.
hints: The base case is anything that is not an object, plus `null`.
Freeze the current object, then recurse into `Object.keys(value)`; this works for arrays too.
Return the original reference. Skipping objects that are already frozen also makes the function safe on structures that refer back to themselves.
guide.brute_force: `Object.freeze(value)` alone. Top-level assignments are blocked; nested ones go straight through.
guide.approach:
Check, freeze, recurse, return.

**Dry run** on `{tags: ["x", "y"]}` with mutations `tags[0] = "z"`, `tags[2] = "new"`, `tags = []`. The outer object is frozen, then the array. In strict mode all three assignments throw: changing an element, adding an element, and replacing the property. `blocked` is 3 and the value is unchanged. With a shallow freeze only the third would be blocked.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(number of nested values); recursion depth equals nesting depth.
guide.pitfalls: `typeof null === "object"`. Forgetting arrays. Returning a frozen copy leaves the original mutable and makes `sameReference` false. Outside strict mode writes to frozen objects fail silently, which is why the driver declares `"use strict"`.
guide.follow_up: Write the matching type: `type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } : T`.

ts-route-params.title: Match a route and extract parameters
ts-route-params.description:
Template literal types can pull parameter names out of a route pattern at compile time
(`"/quays/:quayId"` → `"quayId"`). Web frameworks do the matching job at runtime. Write that matcher.

`matchRoute(pattern, path)` returns an object of captured parameters, or `null` if the path does not match.

Split both strings on `/` and ignore empty segments (so leading, trailing and doubled slashes do not matter). Then
compare segment by segment. A pattern segment is one of:

| pattern segment | matches | captures |
|---|---|---|
| plain text such as `berths` | exactly that text (case-sensitive) | nothing |
| `:name` | any one segment | `name` → that segment |
| `:name?` (only as the last pattern segment) | one segment, or none | `name` → the segment, or no key at all when absent |
| `*` (only as the last pattern segment) | all remaining segments, possibly none | `"*"` → the remaining segments joined with `/` (`""` when none) |

Apart from the optional and wildcard cases the number of segments must be equal. Captured values are the raw text.

**Examples:** `matchRoute("/quays/:quayId/berths/:berthId", "/quays/north/berths/12")` → `{"quayId": "north", "berthId": "12"}` ·
`matchRoute("/files/*", "/files/a/b.txt")` → `{"*": "a/b.txt"}` · `matchRoute("/quays/:id", "/quays")` → `null`

guide.prereqs: Template literal types and the `RouteParams` example (*Type operations*); route parameters in Express (*Typing React and Express*).
guide.intuition: A route is a list of segments. Walk the pattern and the path side by side: text must be equal, a `:name` takes whatever is there and remembers it. The two special endings decide how the lengths may differ.
hints: Normalise both strings with `split("/")` and drop empty parts.
Handle `*` and `:name?` first inside the loop, and only when they are the last pattern segment; each returns immediately.
After the loop the path must have no segments left over.
guide.brute_force: Convert the pattern to a regular expression (`:name` → `([^/]+)`, `*` → `(.*)`) and run it. It is the approach of many routers and is equally fast, but escaping literal text correctly and naming the captures takes care.
guide.approach:
Segment-by-segment comparison with early exits.

**Dry run**: pattern `/quays/:id?`, path `/quays/north/extra`. Segments `[quays, :id?]` and `[quays, north, extra]`. `quays` equals `quays`. `:id?` is last and optional: the path has more than one segment left (length 3 > 2) → `null`. With the path `/quays` the length equals `i` (1), so nothing is captured and `{}` is returned.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(length of pattern + length of path).
guide.pitfalls: Returning a match when the path is longer than the pattern. Storing `undefined` for an absent optional parameter instead of omitting the key. Treating matching as case-insensitive.
guide.follow_up: Decode captured values with `decodeURIComponent`, and write the TypeScript type that derives `{ quayId: string; berthId: string }` from the pattern literal.

ts-combine-object-types.title: Union and intersection of object types
ts-combine-object-types.description:
`A | B` and `A & B` do opposite things to the **properties** you may use, which regularly confuses people:

- on a union `A | B` you can only read properties that exist in **both**, and each has the union of the two types;
- an intersection `A & B` has the properties of **either**, and a shared property has the intersection of the two types.

Model it. An object type is described as a map from property name to a list of type names (the list is a union, for
example `["string", "number"]` means `string | number`).

Write `combine(op, a, b)`:

- `op === "union"`: the result contains only the keys present in both `a` and `b`. Each maps to all names from either
  list, without duplicates.
- `op === "intersection"`: the result contains every key of `a` and of `b`. A key in only one of them keeps its list.
  A shared key maps to the names found in **both** lists; if there are none, it maps to `["never"]`.

Every list in the result is sorted alphabetically.

**Examples:** `combine("union", {"id": ["number"], "name": ["string"]}, {"id": ["string"], "age": ["number"]})` →
`{"id": ["number", "string"]}` · the same with `"intersection"` →
`{"id": ["never"], "name": ["string"], "age": ["number"]}`

guide.prereqs: Unions and intersections of object types (*Objects and structural typing*); `never` (*Type operations*).
guide.intuition: Think in sets of *values*. A union has more values, so fewer properties are guaranteed: only the shared ones. An intersection has fewer values, each of which must satisfy both descriptions: all properties, and shared ones must satisfy both types at once.
hints: For the union loop over one object's keys and keep those the other has.
For the intersection loop over both key lists; treat shared and unshared keys separately.
An empty overlap is the type `never`, written here as `["never"]`.
guide.brute_force: Nested loops over both key lists, comparing names. O(n × m) and correct; own-property lookups make it linear in the number of keys.
guide.approach:
Two branches on `op`, with a small `unique` helper that removes duplicates and sorts.

**Dry run** (intersection) on `a = {id: [number], name: [string]}`, `b = {id: [string], age: [number]}`. `id` is shared: common names of `[number]` and `[string]` → none → `[never]`. `name` only in `a` → `[string]`. `age` only in `b` → `[number]`. This is the lesson's warning made visible: intersecting conflicting property types silently produces `never`.
guide.complexity: Time O(total number of type names × list length), space proportional to the output.
guide.pitfalls: Mixing the two up (keeping all keys for a union). Returning an empty list where `never` is meant. Forgetting to sort or to remove duplicates.
guide.follow_up: A discriminated union is the case where the shared key (`kind`) has different single literals in each member. What does `combine("union", ...)` give for it, and why is that useful for narrowing?

ts-print-type.title: Type descriptor pretty-printer
ts-print-type.description:
Editors show types as text when you hover. Write the function that turns a type **descriptor** into TypeScript syntax.

`printType(type)` returns a string. Descriptors:

| descriptor | prints as |
|---|---|
| a string such as `"string"`, `"number"`, `"unknown"` | itself |
| `{"kind": "literal", "value": v}` | strings with double quotes via `JSON.stringify`; numbers and booleans as they are |
| `{"kind": "array", "element": T}` | `T[]`; if `T` is a union or a function, wrap it: `(A | B)[]` |
| `{"kind": "tuple", "elements": [T, ...]}` | `[A, B]`; empty tuple is `[]` |
| `{"kind": "object", "props": [{"name", "type", "optional"?}, ...]}` | `{ a: A; b?: B }`; no properties prints `{}` |
| `{"kind": "union", "members": [T, ...]}` | members joined with `" | "`; a function member is wrapped in parentheses; an empty union prints `never` |
| `{"kind": "function", "params": [{"name", "type", "optional"?}, ...], "returns": T}` | `(a: A, b?: B) => R` |

Properties and parameters are printed in the order given. Nested types are printed recursively with the same rules.

**Examples:** `printType({"kind":"array","element":{"kind":"union","members":["string","number"]}})` → `"(string | number)[]"` ·
`printType({"kind":"object","props":[{"name":"id","type":"number"},{"name":"tag","type":"string","optional":true}]})` →
`"{ id: number; tag?: string }"`

guide.prereqs: Type syntax for arrays, tuples, objects, unions and functions; why `(A | B)[]` needs parentheses (*Functions, arrays and tuples*).
guide.intuition: A descriptor is a tree, and printing a tree is recursion: print the children, then glue them together with the punctuation of the parent. Parentheses are needed exactly where the parent's punctuation binds tighter than the child's: `[]` binds tighter than `|` and `=>`.
hints: Strings are the base case.
A helper that prints `name?: type` serves both object properties and parameters.
Decide about parentheses in the *parent* (array or union), by looking at the child's `kind`.
guide.brute_force: Wrap every nested type in parentheses. The output is unambiguous and unreadable: `((string) | (number))[]`. The tests expect minimal parentheses.
guide.approach:
A `switch` on `kind` with one line per case.

**Dry run**: array of union `string | number`. The element prints as `string | number`. The parent is an array and the child is a union → wrap → `(string | number)` + `[]`. Without the wrap the text would read as `string | number[]`, a different type.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(size of the descriptor).
guide.pitfalls: Missing parentheses change the meaning. `() => void | undefined` is a function returning a union, so a function inside a union must be wrapped. Empty object and empty union have special spellings. Quotes inside string literals must be escaped, which `JSON.stringify` does.
guide.follow_up: Print long object types across several lines with indentation, as editors do, or parse the text back into a descriptor.

tests.expected: { pos: { lat: number; lon: number }; tags: string[]; on?: (e: string) => void }

ts-safe-json-parse.title: Safe JSON parse with a shape check
ts-safe-json-parse.description:
`JSON.parse(text) as Settings` checks nothing. Write the honest version: parse, verify the shape, and report the
outcome as a discriminated union without ever throwing.

`safeParse(text, shape)`: `shape` maps each expected key to a type tag: `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"array"`,
`"object"` (plain object) or `"null"`. A tag ending in `?` (for example `"number?"`) marks the key as optional.

Return `{"ok": true, "value": parsed}` when everything fits, otherwise `{"ok": false, "error": message}` with the
**first** problem found, checking in this order:

1. the text is not valid JSON → `"invalid JSON"`;
2. the parsed value is not a plain object (it is an array, `null` or a primitive) → `"expected object"`;
3. then for each key of `shape`, in the order given:
   - key absent and required → `"missing key: <key>"`;
   - key absent and optional → fine;
   - key present with the wrong type → `"wrong type for <key>: expected <tag>, got <actual>"`, where `<tag>` is the tag
     without `?` and `<actual>` is `"null"`, `"array"`, or the `typeof` of the value.

Keys not mentioned in `shape` are allowed.

**Examples:** `safeParse('{"port": 8080}', {"port": "number"})` → `{"ok": true, "value": {"port": 8080}}` ·
`safeParse('{"port": "8080"}', {"port": "number"})` → `{"ok": false, "error": "wrong type for port: expected number, got string"}`

guide.prereqs: Why `as` validates nothing, `unknown`, and result unions (*Runtime validation and API response typing*).
guide.intuition: Three gates in a row: is it JSON, is it an object, does each expected key have the expected kind of value. The first gate that fails names the problem; passing all three earns the `ok: true` label.
hints: Wrap `JSON.parse` in `try`/`catch` and return from the `catch`.
A helper `tagOf(v)` returning `null`, `array` or `typeof v` is used for both the object test and the messages.
Test presence with an own-property check: a key holding `null` is present.
guide.brute_force: Call `JSON.parse` and compare `typeof value[key]` directly. It throws on bad text, on `null`, and cannot tell arrays and `null` from objects.
guide.approach:
Parse, check the container, loop over the shape.

**Dry run**: text `{"host": "h", "port": null}`, shape `{host: string, port: number?}`. Valid JSON, a plain object. `host`: present, tag `string` → fine. `port`: optional, but it **is** present, with tag `null` → `wrong type for port: expected number, got null`. Optional means "may be absent", not "may be null".
guide.complexity: Time O(length of text + number of keys), space O(size of parsed value).
guide.pitfalls: Letting the exception escape. `typeof null` and `typeof []`. Treating `null` as absent. Reporting several errors when the first is asked for, or checking keys in the wrong order.
guide.follow_up: Collect all problems with their paths instead of stopping at the first; that is the next problem, *Build a schema validator*.

expected.error: wrong type for port: expected number, got string
wrong type for port: expected number, got null
wrong type for tags: expected array, got object
wrong type for on: expected boolean, got number
wrong type for a: expected string, got number

ts-schema-validate.title: Build a schema validator
ts-schema-validate.description:
Libraries such as Zod describe data with **schemas**: runtime values that can check data and report precisely what is
wrong. Build a small one.

`validate(schema, value)` returns `{"success": true, "data": value}` when there are no problems, otherwise
`{"success": false, "errors": [{"path": ..., "message": ...}, ...]}` listing **every** problem in the order found.

`path` is the location as a dotted string: object keys and array indexes joined with `.`, for example `"roles.1"`;
the root is `""`.

**Schemas**

| schema | rule and messages |
|---|---|
| `{"type": "string", "min"?, "max"?}` | not a string → `expected string`. Then length < min → `string shorter than <min>`; length > max → `string longer than <max>` |
| `{"type": "number", "int"?, "min"?, "max"?}` | not a number → `expected number`. Then, each checked independently and in this order: `int` true and not an integer → `expected integer`; value < min → `number below <min>`; value > max → `number above <max>` |
| `{"type": "boolean"}` | `expected boolean` |
| `{"type": "literal", "value": v}` | value `!== v` → `expected literal ` + `JSON.stringify(v)` |
| `{"type": "array", "element": S, "min"?}` | not an array → `expected array`. Otherwise: length < min → `array shorter than <min>` (at the array's own path); then every element is validated against `S` at `path.index` |
| `{"type": "object", "shape": {key: S}, "strict"?}` | not a plain object → `expected object`. Otherwise each key of `shape`, in order, is validated at `path.key` (a missing key is validated as `undefined`). If `strict` is true, then each own key of the value that is not in `shape`, in the value's key order → `unexpected key` at `path.key` |
| `{"type": "optional", "inner": S}` | `undefined` passes; anything else is validated against `S` |
| `{"type": "nullable", "inner": S}` | `null` passes; anything else is validated against `S` |
| `{"type": "union", "options": [S, ...]}` | passes if at least one option produces no errors; otherwise one error `no union option matched` at this path |

**One global rule, applied first:** if the value is `undefined` (a missing key) and the schema is not `optional`, the
only error is `required` at that path.

**Example:** `validate({"type":"object","shape":{"id":{"type":"number"},"name":{"type":"string"}}}, {"id":"7"})` →
`{"success": false, "errors": [{"path": "id", "message": "expected number"}, {"path": "name", "message": "required"}]}`

guide.prereqs: The miniature schema library and the difference between compile-time types and runtime validation (*Runtime validation and API response typing*); discriminated unions for results.
guide.intuition: A schema is a tree that mirrors the data. Validation walks both trees together. Each node type knows how to check one level and hands the levels below to its children, passing along the path travelled so far. Errors are lists, and a parent's list is the concatenation of its children's.
hints: Write an inner `check(schema, value, path)` that returns an array of errors; an empty array means valid.
Apply the `required` rule at the very top of `check`, before the `switch`.
Containers call `check` on each child with `[...path, key]`; `union` calls it on each option and only looks at whether the result is empty.
guide.brute_force: Return `true`/`false` (a type guard). It is far shorter and tells the caller nothing about *what* is wrong, which is the whole reason schema libraries exist.
guide.approach:
Recursive descent with error accumulation.

**Dry run**: schema `object{id: number, name: string}`, value `{id: "7"}`. Root: a plain object. Key `id`: value `"7"`, not a number → `{path: "id", message: "expected number"}`. Key `name`: absent → validated as `undefined` → global rule → `{path: "name", message: "required"}`. Two errors, `success: false`.

**Union dry run**: `union(literal "circle", literal "rect")` on `"hex"`: option 1 yields an error, option 2 yields an error, no option is clean → one error `no union option matched`; the options' own errors are discarded.
guide.complexity: Time O(size of value × number of union options along the way), space O(depth + number of errors).
guide.pitfalls: Stopping at the first error. `optional` must not accept `null`, and `nullable` must not accept a missing key. `typeof [] === "object"`. Building paths without the parents. Number checks are independent: `3.5` against `int, min 10` reports two errors.
guide.follow_up: In TypeScript, add `type Infer<S>` that derives the static type from a schema with conditional types and `infer`, so one definition gives both the validator and the type.

args.name: A name that is far too long for it

ts-state-machine.title: Run a tagged state machine
ts-state-machine.description:
A data-loading screen is in exactly one state at a time. In TypeScript both the states and the events are discriminated
unions:

```typescript
type State =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading"; attempt: number }
  | { status: "success"; data: unknown }
  | { status: "failure"; error: string; attempts: number };
```

Write `runMachine(events)`. Start in `{ "status": "idle" }`, apply each event, and return the list of states **after
each event** (so the result has the same length as `events`).

| event | allowed from | next state |
|---|---|---|
| `{"type": "fetch"}` | `idle`, `success` | `{"status": "loading", "attempt": 1}` |
| `{"type": "resolve", "data": d}` | `loading` | `{"status": "success", "data": d}` |
| `{"type": "reject", "error": e}` | `loading` | `{"status": "failure", "error": e, "attempts": <the loading attempt>}` |
| `{"type": "retry"}` | `failure` with `attempts` < 3 | `{"status": "loading", "attempt": attempts + 1}` |
| `{"type": "reset"}` | any state | `{"status": "idle"}` |

An event that is not allowed in the current state, or whose `type` is not in the table, leaves the state unchanged
(the unchanged state is still recorded in the output).

**Example:** `runMachine([{"type":"fetch"},{"type":"reject","error":"timeout"},{"type":"retry"}])` →
`[{"status":"loading","attempt":1},{"status":"failure","error":"timeout","attempts":1},{"status":"loading","attempt":2}]`

guide.prereqs: Discriminated unions for states and events (*Interview essentials II*, exercise 7; *Runtime validation and API response typing*).
guide.intuition: A state machine is a table: for each pair (current state, event) there is either a next state or "stay where you are". The code is that table written as a `switch` on the event with a check of the current status inside each case.
hints: Write `transition(state, event)` returning the next state, and return `state` itself when the event is not allowed.
The failure state must remember which attempt failed; read it from the loading state.
Push the state after every event, changed or not.
guide.brute_force: Keep separate flags (`isLoading`, `error`, `data`, `attempts`) and update them per event. That is the design the tagged union replaces: flags can drift into impossible combinations such as loading with an error.
guide.approach:
Fold the events through `transition`, recording each result.

**Dry run**: `fetch, reject a, retry, reject b, retry, reject c, retry, fetch`. States: loading(1), failure(a, 1), loading(2), failure(b, 2), loading(3), failure(c, 3), then `retry` is refused because attempts is 3 → failure(c, 3) again, then `fetch` is not allowed from failure → failure(c, 3).
guide.complexity: Time O(number of events), space O(number of events) for the history.
guide.pitfalls: Transitions that ignore the current state (a late `resolve` overwriting a failure). Forgetting the retry limit. Not recording ignored events. Allowing `fetch` while already loading, which would restart the attempt count.
guide.follow_up: Represent the table as data (`{ idle: { fetch: ... } }`) and write a generic interpreter; libraries such as XState work this way.

ts-function-variance.title: Function assignability and variance
ts-function-variance.description:
When may one function be used in place of another? The practical rule: *a replacement may accept more and return
less.* Implement the check that `strictFunctionTypes` performs.

`isFunctionAssignable(source, target, parents)`:

- A function type is `{"params": [typeName, ...], "returns": typeName}`.
- `parents` maps a type name to its direct supertype, for example `{"Gull": "Bird", "Bird": "Animal"}`. Type `A` is a
  **subtype** of `B` when `A === B` or `B` is reached by following `parents` upward from `A`.

`source` is assignable to `target` when all three hold:

1. **Arity.** `source` has no more parameters than `target` (a function may ignore trailing arguments).
2. **Parameters are contravariant.** For each parameter position `i` of `source`, `target.params[i]` is a subtype of
   `source.params[i]`: the source must accept at least everything the target's callers may pass.
3. **Return type is covariant.** `source.returns` is a subtype of `target.returns`. Special case: if `target.returns`
   is `"void"`, any source return type is accepted.

**Examples** (with `Gull → Bird → Animal`):
`isFunctionAssignable({"params":["Bird"],"returns":"Gull"}, {"params":["Gull"],"returns":"Bird"}, parents)` → `true` ·
`isFunctionAssignable({"params":["Gull"],"returns":"void"}, {"params":["Bird"],"returns":"void"}, parents)` → `false`

guide.prereqs: Variance, the Bird/Gull example and parameter-count compatibility (*Interview essentials I*, *Functions, arrays and tuples*).
guide.intuition: Imagine the code that holds the `target` type. It will call the function with the target's parameter types and use the result as the target's return type. The source must cope with those calls (so its parameters must be at least as wide) and must hand back something usable (so its return must be at least as narrow).
hints: Write `isSubtype(a, b)` by walking up the `parents` map from `a`.
For parameters the arguments to `isSubtype` are swapped compared with the return type.
Fewer source parameters is fine; more is not.
guide.brute_force: Require identical parameter and return types. Simple and safe, but it rejects many valid substitutions, including every callback that ignores an argument.
guide.approach:
Three checks in order: arity, each parameter (contravariant), return (covariant, with the `void` exception).

**Dry run**: source `(Gull) => void`, target `(Bird) => void`. Arity 1 ≤ 1. Parameter 0: is the target's `Bird` a subtype of the source's `Gull`? Walk up from `Bird`: Bird, Animal: no `Gull` → `false`. In words: a holder of the target may pass a penguin, and the source only handles gulls.

**Second**: source `(Bird) => Gull`, target `(Gull) => Bird`. Parameter: `Gull` is a subtype of `Bird` → ok. Return: `Gull` is a subtype of `Bird` → ok → `true`.
guide.complexity: Time O(parameters × height of the hierarchy), space O(height) for the visited set.
guide.pitfalls: Checking parameters in the covariant direction. Demanding equal parameter counts. Forgetting that a `void` target accepts any return. A cycle in `parents` would loop for ever without a visited set.
guide.follow_up: Add a `method: true` flag for which parameters are checked bivariantly (either direction), mirroring TypeScript's exception for method syntax.

ts-deep-partial-merge.title: Deep partial merge
ts-deep-partial-merge.description:
`DeepPartial<T>` describes a patch: any subset of the fields of `T`, at any depth. The matching runtime operation
applies such a patch to a complete object.

Write `mergeDeep(base, patch)` returning a **new** value, without modifying `base` or `patch`:

- If both `base` and `patch` are plain objects (not arrays, not `null`), the result has every key of `base` and every
  key of `patch`. For a key present in `patch`, the result is `mergeDeep(base[key], patch[key])`; keys only in `base`
  are kept.
- In every other case the patch wins: the result is `patch`. That covers primitives, `null` (an explicit `null` in the
  patch overwrites), arrays (replaced as a whole, never merged element by element), and a plain object replacing a
  non-object.

The provided driver `mergeReport(base, patch)` returns `{ "merged": ..., "baseUnchanged": true/false }`, where
`baseUnchanged` tells whether `base` still looks the same afterwards.

**Example:** `mergeDeep({"theme": {"colour": "navy", "size": 14}, "wrap": true}, {"theme": {"size": 16}})` →
`{"theme": {"colour": "navy", "size": 16}, "wrap": true}`

guide.prereqs: `Partial` is shallow; `DeepPartial` and the deep merge sketch (*Interview essentials II*, exercise 11).
guide.intuition: Two plain objects are merged key by key, and the same question is asked again one level down. As soon as either side is anything else, there is nothing to merge and the patch replaces the base.
hints: A helper `isPlain(v)`: an object, not `null`, not an array.
Start the result as a shallow copy of `base`, then overwrite each key that the patch mentions.
Never assign into `base`; the driver checks that it is unchanged.
guide.brute_force: `{ ...base, ...patch }`. One level deep it is right. Below that, a patch of `{theme: {size: 16}}` replaces the whole `theme` object and `colour` disappears.
guide.approach:
Recursive merge returning fresh objects along the patched path.

**Dry run**: base `{a: {b: {c: 1, d: 2}, e: 3}}`, patch `{a: {b: {c: 10}}}`. Both plain → copy base; key `a`: both plain → copy; key `b`: both plain → copy `{c: 1, d: 2}`; key `c`: `1` and `10` are not plain → `10`. Unwinding gives `{a: {b: {c: 10, d: 2}, e: 3}}`. `base` itself was only read.
guide.complexity: Time O(size of patch + number of keys copied along the patched path), space the same.
guide.pitfalls: Mutating `base`. Treating arrays as objects and merging them by index. Ignoring an explicit `null` in the patch. Using truthiness, which would drop a patch value of `0` or `false`.
guide.follow_up: Write the type: `type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T`, and note which of its cases (functions, arrays) need special handling.
